questions.explanation: `//` floors toward negative infinity: -7 // 2 = -4 and 7 // -2 = -4. `%` always takes the sign of the divisor and satisfies a == (a // b) * b + a % b: -7 % 2 = 1 and 7 % -2 = -1. (C and Java truncate toward zero and give different answers.)

questions.explanation: 0.1 and 0.2 have no exact binary representation, so their sum is 0.30000000000000004 and `== 0.3` is False. Rounding to 2 places gives 0.3 exactly, and a tolerance test (`abs(a - b) < 1e-9`, or math.isclose) is the standard way to compare floats.
`~x` is -x - 1, so ~5 = -6 and ~-1 = 0. 5 & 3 = 0b101 & 0b011 = 1, 5 | 3 = 7, 5 ^ 3 = 6. `1 << 4` is 16. `>>` is an arithmetic shift that keeps the sign, so -8 >> 1 = -4. All are O(1) on small ints.

Python ints have unlimited size, so 2**64 is exact (no overflow). It needs 65 bits (2**64 is a 1 followed by 64 zeros). `//` on ints stays exact: 10**20 // 3 has 20 digits. Big-int arithmetic costs more as the numbers grow (roughly O(digits) for addition).

questions.prompt: is_power_of_two(0) returns True. What is the bug?
options: `&` has lower precedence than `==` in Python
0 & (0 - 1) is 0, so the test passes for 0; add the condition n > 0
The expression should use `|` instead of `&`
n - 1 must be written as n >> 1
questions.explanation: A power of two has a single 1 bit, so clearing the lowest set bit with n & (n - 1) leaves 0. But 0 also leaves 0, and negative numbers are not powers of two, so the test needs `n > 0 and n & (n - 1) == 0`. (In Python, & binds tighter than ==.) O(1) time.

questions.prompt: What is the time complexity of this function for a positive integer n with k bits set?
options: O(k)
O(log n) always
O(n)
questions.explanation: `n &= n - 1` clears the lowest set bit, so the loop runs once per set bit: k iterations, at most log₂ n. Counting all bits with a shift loop is always O(log n). Space is O(1).

questions.prompt: Which identity always holds in Python for integers a and b (b != 0)?
options: a // b truncates toward zero and a % b has the sign of a
a % b is always between 0 and abs(b) - 1, whatever the sign of b
a == (a // b) * b + a % b, where a % b has the sign of b
a // b rounds to the nearest integer
questions.explanation: Python floors the quotient and defines the remainder so that the identity holds. For a negative divisor the remainder is zero or negative (7 % -2 == -1). This is why `i % n` is always a valid list index for positive n, even when i is negative.

questions.prompt: How do you imitate a 32-bit signed integer overflow in Python?
options: Python ints wrap around at 2**31 automatically
Python ints never overflow; mask with & 0xFFFFFFFF and convert values at or above 2**31 back to negative yourself
Use the float type, which overflows to inf
Python raises OverflowError for ints above 2**63
questions.explanation: Arbitrary-precision ints grow as needed, so overflow never happens by itself. Bit-manipulation problems that mean 32-bit behaviour need an explicit mask: `x & 0xFFFFFFFF`, then `x - 2**32 if x >= 2**31 else x` to reinterpret as signed.

questions.prompt: You computed total = sum of many prices as floats and need to check that it equals 59.97. Which check is correct?
options: total == 59.97
total is 59.97
str(total) == "59.97"
math.isclose(total, 59.97) or abs(total - 59.97) < 1e-9
questions.explanation: Float addition accumulates tiny rounding errors, so exact equality is unreliable. A tolerance comparison is the standard fix (for money, use integer cents or decimal.Decimal). `is` compares object identity, and string comparison depends on the repr of the rounding error.
